text: PHILIP MORRIS
INCORPORATED
100 PARK AVENUE, NEW YORK, N.Y. 10017
JOSEPH F.CULLMAN, 3RD
CHAIAMAN OF THE BOARD
Dear John:
I would like to comment further on the proposed City
tax on the "tar" and nicotine content of cigarettes which I
understand will soon come before the legislature for consider-
ation. I have outlined to you in my letters of March 8 and
March 24 the strong objections to this measure based both on
the lack of scientific validity of its premise and the extreme
difficulties it would pose from an administrative and marketing
standpoint.
Mr. Malcolm L. Fleischer, Managing Director of the
Retail Tobacco Dealers of America, has recently shown me
your letter to him dated May 5 in which you defend the tax
on two grounds: (1) it is not a tax on all cigarettes and
therefore will not pose a threat to the City's and State's
legitimate cigarette industry by reason of criminal activity;
and (2) it is an attempt "to use the tax structure as an
instrument in the attack on major threats to public health."
Both grounds, it seems to me, are questionable.
The City's own figures indicate that the tax would
apply to over 857 of the cigarettes marketed in New York.
It seems quite certain that an additional 3-cent or 4-cent
tax on 85% of all cigarettes sold in the City would not only
aggravate the problem of bootlegging but also further encourage
out-of-City purchases of the brands subject to the tax. Thus
the City would not only fail to gain the anticipated revenue
from this measure, but in the light of past experience, would
also be likely to suffer a loss in revenue from the present
4 cents per pack excise tax.
The "public health" rationale is totally without
scientific foundation. There is no evidence which establishes
that "tar" and nicotine are significant in terms of human
health or which justifies any distinction on health grounds
between cigarettes with more or less than 17 milligrams of
"tar" and 1.l milligrams of nicotine.
